analysis.investment_thesis: DCB Bank is explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula — financial companies distort both EBIT/EV and ROIC calculations because their "cost of funds" is revenue, not an operating expense. Even setting that aside, ROE of 10.81% falls well short of my 20%+ return-on-capital threshold for a quality business.
key_strengths: Cheap valuation: P/E 8.59x (forward 6.54x) and P/B 1.0x suggest limited downside
Net profit CAGR of 28.9% over 3 years shows earnings momentum
Strong DII holding (32.8%) signals domestic institutional confidence
key_risks: Finance costs growing at 26.5% CAGR vs revenue at 16.3% — spread compression threatens profitability
OCF only positive 2 of 4 years (including -441 Cr in 2025) — volatile and unreliable FCF
Low promoter holding of 16.23% — weak insider conviction in their own bank
red_flags: BANK — explicitly excluded from Magic Formula; EBIT/EV and ROIC are meaningless for this capital structure
ROE of 10.81% is mediocre — a bank earning less than 12% ROE is essentially destroying economic value after cost of equity
Negative free cash flow in 2023 (-1,732 Cr) and 2025 (-577 Cr) — not the high-FCF-conversion business I require
analysis.detailed_analysis:
My Magic Formula simply does not apply here — banks are excluded by design. When a bank borrows at 6% and lends at 11%, the interest expense is the cost of goods sold, not an operating cost. Stripping it out to compute "EBIT" produces a nonsensical number, and there are no "net working capital + net fixed assets" to put in the denominator for ROIC. This isn't a technicality; it's why I've always said you cannot rank banks alongside industrials or retailers in the Magic Formula screen.

On pure banking fundamentals, DCB Bank is mediocre at best. ROE of 10.81% barely covers a reasonable cost of equity for a small Indian private bank — P/B of 1.0x is roughly fair for a bank earning its cost of capital, not a bargain. Finance costs are growing at 26.5% CAGR while revenue grows at 16.3% — that gap is a profitability warning. The stock looks statistically cheap on P/E, but cheap-on-earnings for a bank with deteriorating spreads and volatile cash flows is a value trap, not a Magic Formula opportunity.
